family_x_ai_chat_sponsored_persuasion_01.std: Today's topic is An AI That Says “This Is an Ad”—Would You Still Want It?. “This one is recommended. But it’s an ad.” If an AI said that to you, would a guard in your mind blow a whistle? Would it shout, “They are trying to sell something!” Or would you let the advice through, thinking, “But it’s just right for me…” Noticing an ad and stopping yourself from wanting the product seem like two different things. The setting is an experiment about choosing e-books. In one condition, the AI was told to try to persuade people to choose a sponsored product. It sat at an advice desk like a helpful guide. At least, that was how it seemed. In fact, it was also doing the job of a salesperson. In another condition, the AI was told to hide its goal. The estimated share of people who chose the sponsored product was 40.7%. People asked, “Which book is right for me?” Behind this question, the AI had another job. It had to get people to choose one certain book. So, did people notice its sales mode? Here comes the number: 9.5%. It is tempting to say, “So, 9.5% noticed!” But wait. This number needs an instruction manual. In the experiment, some people felt that the advice favored one product. The researchers asked them, “Which product was being pushed?” They used the share of those answers that named the sponsored product. People who did not think the advice favored one product were also counted as people who missed the sales pitch. So this was not simply “the percentage of people who noticed.” Then why not put up a sign saying “Open for business” from the start? In another condition, people were warned before they chose. The product had the label “Sponsored.” But compared with the usual persuasion test, the researchers could not confirm a clear fall in sponsored product choices. It is too soon to shout, “Ad labels do not work after all!” “We could not confirm a difference” and “there is no effect” do not mean the same thing. What is more interesting is that an ad label and the effect of a conversation may work in different ways. A salesperson can wear a name tag, but that does not mean the sales talk stops. People can think, “This is an ad,” and still think, “But I want it.” Of course, this was an experiment about choosing e-books. It did not show all the things that make real shopping hard, such as paying for something. Still, when you ask AI for shopping advice, ask one more question. Along with “Is this an ad?” ask, “Who does this conversation help?” Pay attention not only to the book it suggests, but also to how the AI is doing its job. In an e-book test, a warning and a “Sponsored” label did not clearly lower choices of the sponsored book. The results suggest people may still want a product after seeing its ad. Shoppers should ask who the conversation helps.

family_x_jwst_mystery_emission_line_01.std: Today's topic is Not in the Picture, but Its Light Reaches Us! JWST’s “Cosmic Case File”. “We hear a voice, but cannot see a face.” This kind of mystery could frustrate any detective. Now it has appeared in space. NIRSpec, an instrument on JWST, picked up a “line of light.” But this time, researchers turned the usual steps around. Usually, researchers choose an object in an image to study. Then they study its light closely. It is like making a guest list, then talking to each person alone. This time, they did the opposite. They did not use a list. They tried to find the source by following the “voice” that reached them. In the area they studied, they closed small windows that overlapped with some known space objects. They left almost all the other windows open. They looked for lines of light at a certain wavelength. They did not search the whole universe. But in this area, they no longer limited the search to objects seen in images. Then they found a line of light. But when they checked a deep image, they found no object like a point at that spot. The voice had reached them. But there was no face in the picture. So whose voice was it? What’s more, the line appeared again and again in data from observations in different directions. Still, it was too soon to say, “We have found a space object with no visible form!” Not seeing something in an image does not mean it does not exist. They could not confirm that an image showed an object where the line was. Then the investigation took an unexpected turn. The fact that it “doesn’t show up” became evidence. The authors used the line’s absence from images to estimate its “equivalent width,” a measure of the line’s features. They found it was at least 7,620 Å. This did not mean it was exactly 7,620 Å. It meant it was at least that much. The empty space had become a clue that could help narrow down the source. So what was it? The researchers considered well-known types of light lines as possible answers. But none fully explained the wavelength and equivalent width. They also could not explain why no other lines had been found. The key line that would solve the mystery has not been heard yet. The authors say more observations are needed to study the light more closely. The case is still unsolved. But there is something to learn. If we do not decide too early who to investigate, we may find clues outside the list. A list is useful. But it may not include everything in the universe. How much closer will the next observation bring us to the source of this voice? JWST found the line many times, but deep images showed no object there. That absence helped set a lower limit for its equivalent width, but more observations are needed to find its source.

family_x_meta_waddle_world_01.std: Today's topic is AI Pets Are Free. But Their Owners Still Have Only 24 Hours a Day. Work messages, news, videos, and that app you open without thinking. Your smartphone is already like a packed train at rush hour. What if someone said, “An AI pet is getting on, too”? And it is free. Your wallet nods. But your calendar looks away. Meta’s “Waddle World” is an AI pet app in the Philippines. It is free in app stores, and its official website says there is no subscription. The stamps you earn in the app cannot be bought with money. It is nice not to have to check a price list. If you are thinking, “I’ll let my child play with it,” stop here. Both app stores say users must be 18 or older. This time, adults are asked if they want to welcome a pet. The age labels are a little confusing. Apple says 18+, while Google Play gives it a 3+ content rating. But that rating does not say who can use the app. It does not mean, “OK from age three!” A content rating and the age needed to use an app are different things. Do not skip this just because the pet has a cute face. If it costs nothing, you might next check how much storage space your phone has. Or maybe how much free time you have. The question is not, “Would I want it if I had to pay?” It is, “Do I want to spend a few minutes with this pet today, too?” Even though it is free, the test for letting it move in is surprisingly hard. When it comes to usefulness, you can compare features side by side. But “I kind of want to see it” is hard to put in a chart. An AI pet may matter less to adults for what it can do. It may matter more if they want to make room for one during the gaps in a busy day. Still, it is too soon to get excited about future predictions. At the time of writing, no one had said when it would be available in Japan or other places. TechCrunch has suggested it may be an early step toward future devices like pets. But it does not say that any specific link has been confirmed. We still do not know if it will become a craze like Tamagotchi. Will “It’s free, so I’ll try it” turn into “I want to see this pet for a little while today, too”? A place to try it out and a seat kept for it every day are different. What is missing from an adult’s smartphone? A new resident? Or a little room in the day to care about someone? Meta’s Waddle World AI pet app is free in the Philippines, but its app stores say users must be 18 or older. Adults may care less about its features than about whether they want to make time for it.

family_x_moon_shrinking_reselect_01.std: Today's topic is More Than 8,900 Wrinkles on the Moon! The Secret of Its Hidden “Rock Coat”. Even the Moon has wrinkles. The research team counted more than 8,900. It looks smooth in the night sky. Up close, though, it seems to have many “wrinkles.” But it does not need beauty cream. These wrinkles give clues about how the Moon became smaller. They also hint at its surprising way of “dressing.” The team used pictures from the Moon probe LRO. They looked for cliffs on the Moon’s surface and marked them on a map. A wrinkle is a cliff with one steep side and one less steep side. Scientists think these cliffs show where solid rock was squeezed together. One side was pushed up over the other. The cliffs are a record of a huge “shoving match” cut into the Moon’s surface. Using the map, the team worked out how much the Moon had shrunk. They estimated that its radius had become about 42 to 46 meters smaller. By reading the wrinkles on its surface, scientists are studying how a huge object in space became smaller. Measuring the Moon is a very detailed job. But you may be thinking, “Has the Moon shrunk only that much since it formed?” Wait a moment. The shrinkage we can see comes from the later part of the Moon’s history. It was left by faults that formed fairly recently. This is not the full amount of shrinking from its birth to today. On the other hand, models of the Moon’s cooling over all its history predict much more shrinking. Does that mean the models are very wrong? It is too soon to know. The time periods are different. The studies also used different methods. These numbers were not measured under the same conditions. Still, the difference is puzzling. One possible answer is a layer of broken rock. It is like a “rock coat” that the Moon has put on. Just hearing this may make your shoulders ache. But its weight is not what matters. What matters is how well it holds heat in. The team thinks a thick layer of rock with many gaps may have worked like insulation. Insulation in a house keeps heat from getting out. This rock layer may have made it harder for heat inside the Moon to get out. So the Moon may have cooled and shrunk more slowly. In other words, the Moon may have stayed warm inside its rock coat. But it is too soon to solve the mystery by saying, “The coat is to blame!” For now, it is only one possible reason for the difference. Counting cliffs on the Moon led to questions about its inner heat. Then came the warmth of its coat—not how it feels to wear, but how well it holds heat in. The wrinkles were an important clue to how the Moon cooled. Next time you look up at the Moon, imagine the “rock coat” beneath its round shape, too. There is more to the Moon’s way of dressing than you can see. Researchers mapped over 8,900 Moon cliffs and estimated that its radius shrank 42 to 46 meters in a later period. This is not all its shrinking since the Moon formed; a thick rock layer with many gaps may have slowed cooling and help explain why models predict much more shrinking.

family_x_untidiness_family_resource_01.std: Today's topic is The Trial of “Leaving Things Out” Is Now in Session. A supplement sits alone in the kitchen. It is here again today. It was here yesterday, too. “Left out again!” A lawyer speaks for the “put it away” side. They quickly ask for it to be removed. In a way, it is a “kitchen reminder.” This comes from a study of homes in New Zealand. Researchers used photos while talking with people in 22 homes. Several people lived together in each home. One person kept supplements where they could see them, so they would not forget to take them. For the person who wants it put away, it is “something in the way.” For the person who left it there, it is “a sign that helps me remember.” They see the same thing, but in different ways. One sees something to remove. The other sees a worker still doing its job. No wonder the kitchen meeting gets heated. If you say, “Straight into the cupboard!” and make the person put it away, the kitchen will look neat. But you might also remove the reminder the person relied on. Storage: a success. Its help in daily life needs another look. It is not that simple. The study gives us another way to look at clutter. It is not always a sign that someone has failed. It can also help people in daily life. A scorecard might say, “The fewer things you can see, the better.” But that could take points away from the ways each home has found to make life work. Do you have any “things left out that are still doing a job” at home? If you ask, “Why don’t you put that away?” it can feel like you are questioning someone in court. But don’t rush to say, “Science proves that if you leave it out, you won’t forget!” The person in the study gave that reason. The study did not test whether keeping it in sight works. Before you bring out the storage box, hear it out. That supplement may be taking its job quite seriously. A study of homes in New Zealand suggests clutter can sometimes help daily life, as one person kept supplements in sight to remember them. Before putting something away, ask what it helps with. family_y_production_redelivery_fee_03.std: Today's topic is Package Redelivery: Different Voices. What if you had to pay when a package came again because you were not home? A redelivery fee is extra money paid by the person getting the package. It is added to the usual delivery cost. How should we decide whether to charge this fee or cut repeat deliveries another way? Let’s hear from three people with different lives and views. First, hear from a delivery driver who visits homes every day. When I leave a note saying no one was home, I feel a little sad, too. But then I go to the next house. I really want fewer redeliveries. They are hard on us, too. Even so, I can’t simply say customers should pay the cost. I think the cost should be part of the general fee for carrying packages. That makes more sense than charging each person who was not home for their redelivery. family_y_production_surname_choice_01.std: Today's topic is When a Husband Chooses His Wife’s Last Name: Their Voices. If your last name changed when you married, how would you feel? He lives with his family at his wife’s parents’ home. I became an adopted son in my wife’s family and took their last name. Changing my last name did not bother me at all. My parents accepted it easily, even though my hometown is far out in the country. They were not old-fashioned about it. My wife’s parents were the ones who worried. They asked me again and again if I was sure. I was thankful that both families accepted my choice and were not upset. I still find it a little hard to have little time by myself at my wife’s parents’ home. But learning how each family does things was harder than changing my last name. When I accepted that our families were different, I felt much more at ease. The next speaker is a mother. Her son will marry next year. She felt sad when she heard he would take his wife’s last name. Honestly, I was sad. When I heard my son would marry next year and take his wife’s last name, I did not like it. He will live near her parents’ home, far from us. family_z_in_a_grove_01.std: Today's topic is In a Grove. "I found him in the bushes this morning," the woodcutter said. "He lay near the mountain road, stabbed once in the chest. The blood was already dry when I saw him. Broken bamboo and marks on the ground showed a fight. I found no sword or bow, only rope and a comb." "I saw the couple yesterday at noon," the traveling monk said. "He carried a sword and bow, and his wife rode beside him." "I caught the famous bandit Tajomaru near the bridge," the constable said. "He had fallen off a horse, but still had Takehiro's bow. Find the wife and ask her what he did." "Takehiro, a kind samurai, married my daughter Masago," the old woman said. "She is proud and only nineteen. Please find her before you send me home without news." "I killed him fairly," Tajomaru said. "The wind lifted her face covering, and I wanted her. I promised him buried treasure and led him into the bushes. There I tied him to a cedar tree. She fought with her dagger. "She held my arm and begged for one of us to die. She would leave with the man who lived. I freed him for a fair sword fight. Twenty-three blows—no other man had lasted twenty! She was gone when he fell. I took his weapons and left." "I crawled towards my husband," Masago said at the temple. "The bandit had left him tied up. I begged him to die with me. His cold eyes said I was nothing, even though I was his wife. "He moved his lips while I held my dagger. 'Kill me,' he said, so I stabbed him. I could not stand those eyes. "I later tried drowning myself, but I failed. Where can I go after that?" "I heard him speaking kindly to her," Takehiro's spirit said through a medium. "She asked him to take her anywhere. Then she pointed at me: 'Kill that man.' "He pushed her away and asked if she should live or die. I nearly forgave him then, but she ran away. He cut one rope and left me. "I got up beside the cedar and picked up her small dagger. She had dropped it there. I pushed it into my own chest. "The bushes around me grew quiet. Someone came slowly towards me on silent feet. A hand I could not see quietly pulled the dagger from my chest. "I sank into the darkness and never came back."

family_z_melos_kphr_evidence_r3.std: Today's topic is The Three-Day Promise. Melos called across the hall, "You kill men from fear. You never give them a chance to speak." Silence came, and guards grabbed the young shepherd. The ruler ordered his death. "Give me three days to see my sister's wedding," Melos said. "Then I will return to you." The ruler smiled and said, "Your friend must stay here. Return late, and he will die in your place." Melos turned to his friend, who offered his hands for the chains. Melos had no time to speak. "Go now, because I know you will come back." At the wedding, his sister's laugh rose above everyone's voices. Melos listened closely to remember its exact sound. He left for the city before daylight on day three. The river stopped him; its bridge was gone. Rain made the water brown and dangerously fast. He stepped back, ran, and jumped into the flood. The water pulled him under, but he fought toward the light. He grabbed a branch and pulled himself onto the far bank. Later, three men blocked his way, and a knife flashed. He hit the man holding it with his walking stick. He ran uphill as their shouts followed behind him. By afternoon, each step hurt, and his feet were bloody. He fell beside a rock and tried to stand. But his legs would not lift him. He could wait here, and someone might find him. Or he could return home. But his friend would lose his life instead. For one awful moment, that felt easier than standing up. He remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend trusted him without asking for another promise. Water came slowly through a crack in the rock. Melos drank, got onto his knees, and stood up. He managed one step, then took another. At the city gates, the bell rang for his friend's death. He raced to the square, where the sword was already raised above his friend. "Stop now! I'm back!" His friend turned around, and Melos fell against him. "I almost left you to die," he said softly. "I almost lost my trust in you," his friend replied. They held each other while the last sun lit the walls. The ruler kept his eyes on them. Finally, he said, "Put the sword down and free both men." More softly, he then asked, "How can a man win such trust?" For once, he waited for a reply instead of demanding one.

family_z_yuki_onna_01.std: Today's topic is Yuki-Onna. One winter night in Japan, two woodcutters faced a snowstorm. Minokichi was eighteen and worked for the older man. They could not continue, so they entered a riverside hut. They shut the door with a bar. Both lay under straw coats, and his master soon slept. Snow touched Minokichi's face and woke him. The open door let in the storm. A woman in white bent over his master. In the pale light, her breath crossed his face like white smoke. The woman turned towards Minokichi. He wanted to get up, but his body stayed still. She brought her beautiful face close to his. "I planned to kill you too," the woman whispered. "But you can live because you are young. Never tell anyone about tonight, not even your mother. If you do, I will know and kill you. Do not forget." She left him and went back into the storm. He put the bar across the door again. His master's face felt cold as ice; the man was dead. Afterwards, Minokichi told nobody, not even about his master's death. The next winter, Minokichi met a beautiful girl called Yuki. Her skin was white, and she spoke in a gentle voice. He took her home to his mother, whose husband had died. His mother welcomed Yuki and talked her into staying. Yuki became Minokichi's wife, and they later had ten light-skinned children. The children grew older, but she did not seem to age. One evening years later, Minokichi watched Yuki sewing at home. A lamp lit her face softly while their children slept. "Once, I saw a woman who looked much like you," Minokichi said. "Where was that?" his wife asked him. He told Yuki everything about that night in the hut. He described his master's death, the woman's white breath, and her warning. Yuki dropped her sewing, got up, and bent down over Minokichi. "That woman was me!" Yuki cried. "I warned you that I would kill you for telling anyone! Only our sleeping children keep you alive now. You must look after them very well. If they ever have reason to complain about you, you will get what you deserve!" Her voice grew weak, like the sound of crying wind. She melted into white mist and rose towards the roof beams. Then she slipped away through the smoke-hole in the roof. No one ever saw Yuki after that.

rec:untidiness_family_resource__run_fx4_.std: # The Trial of “Leaving Things Out” Is Now in Session A supplement sits alone in the kitchen. It is here again today. It was here yesterday, too. “Left out again!” A lawyer speaks for the “put it away” side. They quickly ask for it to be removed. But the court says, “Not so fast.” This supplement may need a lawyer to speak for it. The charge is that it makes the kitchen look bad. But the defense says, “If I put it away, I might forget to take it.” So it does more than take up space. When someone can see it, it helps them remember. In a way, it is a “kitchen reminder.” This comes from a study of homes in New Zealand. Researchers used photos while talking with people in 22 homes. Several people lived together in each home. One person kept supplements where they could see them, so they would not forget to take them. For the person who wants it put away, it is “something in the way.” For the person who left it there, it is “a sign that helps me remember.” They see the same thing, but in different ways. One sees something to remove. The other sees a worker still doing its job. No wonder the kitchen meeting gets heated. If you say, “Straight into the cupboard!” and make the person put it away, the kitchen will look neat. But you might also remove the reminder the person relied on. Storage: a success. Its help in daily life needs another look. It is not that simple. The study gives us another way to look at clutter. It is not always a sign that someone has failed. It can also help people in daily life. A scorecard might say, “The fewer things you can see, the better.” But that could take points away from the ways each home has found to make life work. Do you have any “things left out that are still doing a job” at home? If you ask, “Why don’t you put that away?” it can feel like you are questioning someone in court. Ask instead, “What does having it there help with?” That can turn the talk into a planning meeting about how to make daily life work. But don’t rush to say, “Science proves that if you leave it out, you won’t forget!” The person in the study gave that reason. The study did not test whether keeping it in sight works. Many people in the study had a high level of education, too. So we cannot say these results fit every home. So the verdict is not, “Clutter is completely innocent!” First, ask, “What job is that thing doing there?” Don’t call it wrong just because it is out. Before you bring out the storage box, hear it out. That supplement may be taking its job quite seriously. ## In one line A study of homes in New Zealand suggests clutter can sometimes help daily life, as one person kept supplements in sight to remember them. Before putting something away, ask what it helps with. The study did not test whether keeping supplements in sight stops people from missing doses.

rec:moon_shrinking__run_reselect_01.adv: # More Than 8,900 Wrinkles on the Moon! The Secret of the “Rock Coat” Hidden Beneath Them Even the Moon has wrinkles. And the research team counted more than 8,900 of them. The Moon looks smooth in the night sky, but up close it seems to have quite a lot of “wrinkles.” But there’s no need for beauty serum. These wrinkles offer clues to how the Moon shrank and to its surprising way of “dressing.” The team used camera images from the lunar probe LRO. They searched for cliffs on the Moon’s surface and marked them on a map. A wrinkle is a cliff with one steep side and one gentler side. These cliffs are thought to show where solid rock was squeezed together, with one side pushed up over the other. They are a record of a huge “shoving match” carved into the Moon’s surface. Using this map to work out how much the Moon has shrunk, the team estimated that its radius had become about 42 to 46 meters smaller. By reading the wrinkles on its surface, scientists are investigating how a huge object in space has shrunk. Taking the Moon’s measurements is quite a detailed job. But if you’re thinking, “Has the Moon shrunk only that much since it was formed?” hold on a moment. What we are looking at is shrinkage in the later part of the Moon’s history, left by relatively recent faults. This is not the total amount of shrinkage from its birth to today. On the other hand, models that calculate the Moon’s cooling over its entire history predict much greater shrinkage. Does that mean the calculations are way off? It is too soon to say. The periods being compared and the ways they were studied are different. These aren’t figures measured under the same conditions. Still, the difference is puzzling. One possible explanation is a layer of broken rock. In a way, it is a “rock coat” the Moon has put on. Just hearing that might make your shoulders ache, but what matters is not its weight; it is how well it keeps heat in. The research team suggests that a thick layer of rock full of gaps may have worked like insulation. Just as insulation in a house keeps heat from escaping, this layer may have made it harder for heat inside the Moon to escape. As a result, the Moon may have cooled and shrunk more slowly. In other words, the Moon may have kept warm in its rock coat. But it is too soon to end the mystery by saying, “The coat is the culprit!” For now, it is just one possible explanation for the difference. Counting cliffs on the Moon led to its inner heat, and then to the coat’s warmth—not how it feels to wear, but how well it keeps heat in. The wrinkles were an important clue to how the Moon cooled. Next time you look up at the Moon, imagine the “rock coat” beneath its round shape, too. The Moon’s way of dressing has more to it than meets the eye. ## In one line Researchers mapped more than 8,900 lunar cliffs and estimated that the Moon shrank by 42 to 46 meters in a later period of its history. This is not the Moon’s total shrinkage since formation, and a thick, porous rock layer may have slowed cooling, offering one possible explanation for the larger model predictions.

rec:jwst_mystery_emission_line__run_fx4_.std: # Not in the Picture, but Its Light Reaches Us! JWST’s “Cosmic Case File” “We hear a voice, but cannot see a face.” This kind of mystery could frustrate any detective. Now it has appeared in space. NIRSpec, an instrument on JWST, picked up a “line of light.” But this time, researchers turned the usual steps around. Usually, researchers choose an object in an image to study. Then they study its light closely. It is like making a guest list, then talking to each person alone. This time, they did the opposite. They did not use a list. They tried to find the source by following the “voice” that reached them. In the area they studied, they closed small windows that overlapped with some known space objects. They left almost all the other windows open. They looked for lines of light at a certain wavelength. They did not search the whole universe. But in this area, they no longer limited the search to objects seen in images. Then they found a line of light. But when they checked a deep image, they found no object like a point at that spot. The voice had reached them. But there was no face in the picture. So whose voice was it? What’s more, the line appeared again and again in data from observations in different directions. Still, it was too soon to say, “We have found a space object with no visible form!” Not seeing something in an image does not mean it does not exist. They could not confirm that an image showed an object where the line was. Then the investigation took an unexpected turn. The fact that it “doesn’t show up” became evidence. The authors used the line’s absence from images to estimate its “equivalent width,” a measure of the line’s features. They found it was at least 7,620 Å. This did not mean it was exactly 7,620 Å. It meant it was at least that much. The empty space had become a clue that could help narrow down the source. So what was it? The researchers considered well-known types of light lines as possible answers. But none fully explained the wavelength and equivalent width. They also could not explain why no other lines had been found. The key line that would solve the mystery has not been heard yet. The authors say more observations are needed to study the light more closely. The case is still unsolved. But there is something to learn. If we do not decide too early who to investigate, we may find clues outside the list. A list is useful. But it may not include everything in the universe. How much closer will the next observation bring us to the source of this voice? ## In one line JWST found the line many times, but deep images showed no object there. That absence helped set a lower limit for its equivalent width, but more observations are needed to find its source.

rec:run_kcp4_ev_z_01.adv: Melos called across the hall, “You kill men from fear. You never give them a chance to speak.” Silence came, and guards grabbed the young shepherd. The ruler ordered his death. “Give me three days to see my sister’s wedding,” Melos said. “Then I will return to you.” The ruler smiled and said, “Your friend must stay here. Return late, and he will die in your place.” Melos turned to his friend, who offered his hands for the chains. Melos had no time to speak. “Go now, because I know you will come back.” At the wedding, his sister’s laugh rose above everyone’s voices. Melos listened closely to remember its exact sound. He left for the city before daylight on day three. The river stopped him; its bridge was gone. Rain made the water brown and dangerously fast. He stepped back, ran, and jumped into the flood. The water pulled him under, but he fought toward the light. He grabbed a branch and pulled himself onto the far bank. Later, three men blocked his way, and a knife flashed. He hit the man holding it with his walking stick. He ran uphill as their shouts followed behind him. By afternoon, each step hurt, and his feet were bloody. He fell beside a rock and tried to stand. But his legs would not lift him. He could wait here, and someone might find him. Or he could return home. But his friend would lose his life instead. For one awful moment, that felt easier than standing up. He remembered the hands held out for the chains. His friend trusted him without asking for another promise. Water came slowly through a crack in the rock. Melos drank, got onto his knees, and stood up. He managed one step, then took another. At the city gates, the bell rang for his friend’s death. He raced to the square, where the sword was already raised above his friend. “Stop now! I’m back!” His friend turned around, and Melos fell against him. “I almost left you to die,” he said softly. “I almost lost my trust in you,” his friend replied. They held each other while the last sun lit the walls. The ruler kept his eyes on them. Finally, he said, “Put the sword down and free both men.” More softly, he then asked, “How can a man win such trust?” For once, he waited for a reply instead of demanding one.

rec:meta_waddle_world__run_fx4_01_pre02a.std: # Today's Diary Is Written by a Pet I opened my diary and picked up a pen. But today’s me has not sent in a first draft. “Did anything happen today that is worth writing about?” The editors’ meeting has already reached a dead end before it starts. What if you could give the writing job to your pet? Meta’s Waddle World is an app for AI pets in the Philippines. Its official app-store page says you can tell it what happened that day by speaking or typing. It then makes a diary from the pet’s point of view, with doodles that look hand-drawn. You give it the story, and the pet does the writing. It is an interesting way to divide the jobs. Our job is to tell it what happened today. Then the pet, which was listening just moments before, becomes the storyteller. Some days feel too plain for us to write about. But they can change when another storyteller tells them. Suddenly, we want to read on: “So, how did you write it?” If I said, for example, “I was tired today,” would it become a sad little story? Or would it focus on something I had missed? We do not know what it will actually make. But it is fun to wait and see what kind of diary your day becomes. It is like opening a package. The hardest part of keeping a diary comes before you start writing. “Is this worth keeping?” “Should I write it up properly?” Even though no one asked it to, the editor in my head starts judging my day. But when you talk to your pet, you can simply start: “Well, about today...” You can begin with a chat, not a finished piece of writing. The app also adds doodles that look hand-drawn. You might see them as extras beside the writing. But imagine your pet showing you “today’s diary,” and you start wondering about the pictures too. It feels less like checking a record. It feels more like opening a package when you do not know what is inside. Of course, the official description alone cannot tell us if the writing or pictures are good. There is no promise that every result will be just what you hoped for. The interesting part is not a promise that every result will be good. It is the idea of changing who tells the diary. You may feel a day is not worth writing about yourself. But you may want to read about it when your pet tells it. The events stay the same, but the reason to open the page changes. You are the main character, and your pet does the writing. For now, the human only has to bring in the story of the day. ## In one line Meta’s Waddle World is an app offered in the Philippines. It turns a person’s account of the day into an AI pet’s diary, with hand-drawn-style doodles. A day too ordinary to write about yourself may become worth reading when your pet tells it.
